assessment.nobel_worthiness: Optical lattice clocks, built on Katori's magic-wavelength proposal and realized with strontium and ytterbium, brought fractional uncertainty to the 1e-18 level. They are the clearest case of a new measurement technique that opens new ways of observing nature: relativistic geodesy, tests of fundamental constants, searches for dark matter and a path to redefining the second. The advance is concrete and quantitative (stability, systematic uncertainty, cross-comparisons), which is the kind of evidence I trust.
assessment.attribution: Katori proposed the magic-wavelength lattice concept and made early demonstrations; Jun Ye's group drove the record stability and accuracy and the many-body clock and comparison work. Two laureates is a natural fit. Others, such as Pierre Lemonde, Hall and Hänsch, were recognized earlier or sit outside the supplied credit, so I take only the supplied names.
assessment.maturity: Multiple independent labs (JILA, RIKEN/Tokyo, SYRTE, PTB, NIST) reproduce clocks at the 1e-18 level and compare them, so confirmation is strong. Recognition is timely, with the redefinition of the second under discussion.
uncertainties: Whether the committee sees this as too close to the 2005 and 2012 clock and precision-measurement prizes
Allocation between Katori and Ye versus other clock groups in the broader field

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Optical detection and coherent control of single colour-centre spins, especially the NV centre in diamond, created a platform for nanoscale quantum sensing of magnetic fields, temperature and strain, as well as for room-temperature qubits and spin-photon interfaces. As a measurement method it reaches single-spin sensitivity and is now used in materials science, biology and geophysics. This is a strong match to the criterion of enabling new observations.
assessment.attribution: Wrachtrup and Jelezko made the first single-NV optical detection and coherent control; Awschalom led the broader colour-centre work, including SiC and divacancy spins and quantum-control demonstrations. Lukin is a major contributor (sensing, quantum registers) but is credited in other candidates here. Because the list has four names, three have to be chosen and the choice of omitted name is a real attribution difficulty.
assessment.maturity: Many independent groups reproduce the results, and commercial sensors exist, so maturity is high. The field is still growing, but the core discovery is stable.
uncertainties: Omitting Lukin, or one of the other three, is contestable
Boundary between the discovery of single-spin detection and the later sensing applications
Which material platform (diamond NV versus SiC) deserves primary credit

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Cirac and Zoller's 1995 proposal for a trapped-ion quantum gate, combined with the experimental realization of entanglement, gates and error-correction-level control with ion strings, defines a leading quantum-computing architecture. It combines theory with demonstration and rests on exceptionally precise laser control of coherence, which I know well from rare-earth-ion work.
assessment.attribution: Cirac and Zoller made the decisive theoretical proposal; Blatt's Innsbruck group did much of the experimental realization of entangled ion strings. Wineland and Haroche already received the 2012 prize for ion and photon control, so the experimental credit (Wineland's NIST group, Monroe, Blatt) is partly spoken for. A fair configuration is plausible but not clean.
assessment.maturity: Multiple groups (Innsbruck, NIST, Maryland, Quantinuum, Oxford) show the platform at high fidelities, so confirmation is strong. Full-scale quantum computing is still an open goal, which makes the timing borderline.
uncertainties: Overlap with the 2012 prize
Whether the credit should be split between the proposal and the experimental platform
Cirac and Zoller also appear in other candidates (lattice simulation, Rydberg), so credit across themes could be consolidated differently

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Programmable Rydberg-atom arrays use optical tweezers and Rydberg blockade to create controllable, strongly interacting many-body systems with single-site readout, used for quantum simulation, ordered phases, and gate operations with neutral atoms. The technique is a genuine new instrument, and several recent demonstrations of error-corrected logical qubits make the impact tangible.
assessment.attribution: Saffman contributed early Rydberg-gate proposals; Browaeys and Lukin led the early tweezer-array experiments and the many-body simulation work. This fits three laureates, but other groups (Bernien, Endres, Kaufman, Weiss, Regal, Browaeys) are also key, and the credit among them is not fully settled.
assessment.maturity: Reproduced by several groups and now commercialized, but the field is young and the leading demonstrations are recent. Interpretation is stable. This may be a few years early.
uncertainties: Premature timing relative to older candidates
Crowded field means the three-person limit leaves out other major experimental contributors
Distinction between tweezer-array technology and Rydberg-blockade physics

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Ultracold atoms in optical lattices, following the Jaksch-Zoller Hubbard-model proposal, allowed the Mott insulator transition and later quantum gas microscopes with single-site resolution. They create tunable analogue simulators for many-body physics, a clear instrument-driven advance with wide influence across condensed matter and AMO.
assessment.attribution: Greiner (with Bloch and Hänsch) did the 2002 superfluid-Mott-insulator transition; Zoller and Cirac supplied the theoretical programme; Bloch led the quantum gas microscope and subsequent simulation work. Cirac is credited but I choose to propose Zoller since Cirac features in B020 and the Hubbard proposal was Jaksch-Zoller. This choice is debatable.
assessment.maturity: Highly reproduced across many groups, with a stable interpretation. Recognition is timely and arguably overdue, though the 2001 BEC prize and 2012 prize cover adjacent ground.
uncertainties: Credit split between Hänsch, Jaksch and others who are not in the supplied list
Whether quantum simulation has produced results that settle open problems in condensed matter yet
Overlap with other AMO candidates

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Circuit QED brought cavity-QED strong coupling to superconducting qubits, providing dispersive readout, microwave photon control and the architecture used in today's superconducting quantum processors. It is the engineering and measurement framework for much of current quantum hardware.
assessment.attribution: Blais, Wallraff and Schoelkopf wrote the 2004 theory and the first strong-coupling demonstration, and have led its development since. The three-person division is natural. Devoret, Martinis and Clarke were just recognized in 2025 for superconducting-circuit macroscopic quantum effects, so Nobel-committee overlap is a concern.
assessment.maturity: Strongly confirmed across many labs and now industrial. The prize for macroscopic quantum tunnelling in circuits in 2025 makes timing for a second superconducting-circuit award less likely in the near term.
uncertainties: Overlap with the recent 2025 prize
Separation of foundational discovery from engineering development

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene revealed correlated insulators and unconventional superconductivity in a tunable, clean system, opening the moiré-materials field. The experimental demonstration and the theoretical flat-band prediction together form a clear, high-impact discovery.
assessment.attribution: Bistritzer and MacDonald predicted the magic angle and flat bands in 2011; Jarillo-Herrero's group observed correlated insulators and superconductivity in 2018. This is a clean theory-plus-experiment configuration. Dean, Yazdani, Young and others contributed key follow-ups.
assessment.maturity: Reproduced by many groups, but the nature of the superconductivity is still debated and sample-to-sample variation remains. Recognition is arguably timely, though the field is still maturing.
uncertainties: Pairing mechanism of the superconductivity is unresolved
Sample reproducibility and twist-angle disorder
Whether the field has yet delivered a stable physical principle

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The discovery of the Higgs boson at the LHC confirmed the last missing piece of the Standard Model, and relied on remarkable detector and measurement instrumentation (calorimetry, tracking, triggering) that I respect. Its scientific importance is very high.
assessment.attribution: Credit is hard: the discovery was made by thousands of collaborators in two experiments. The supplied names are the proposers and early leaders of ATLAS and CMS, and they could support a prize to the detector concepts and leadership, but the statutes and the question of who made the decisive contribution are difficult to resolve. Higgs and Englert were recognized in 2013 for the theory.
assessment.maturity: Confirmed independently by two experiments with a well-characterized signal and properties still being measured, so maturity is very high. Timing is no obstacle.
uncertainties: Large collaboration credit makes a fair three-person allocation contested
The theory was already recognized in 2013
Whether leadership roles equal decisive scientific contribution
